figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: MOST structures policy-internal memory around object states and task progress for long-horizon mobile manipulation. We evaluate it on RoboCasa365, our newly introduced RoboCasa-Long benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage tasks, and real-world deployment. M-Raw in the plots denotes MOST-Raw, a matched visual-history memory variant without task-state supervision or future prediction. Across these settings, MOST outperforms both the memoryless Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1) baseline and MOST-Raw.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: MOST overview. MOST integrates a Vision Language Model, a Memory Expert, and an Action Expert within one end-to-end policy. The Vision Language Model encodes the current observation and instruction. The Memory Expert represents sampled history as object states and task progress, and the Action Expert uses both contexts to generate continuous actions. Task-state supervision is training-only.
figures.headline: MOST combines a Vision Language Model, a Memory Expert, and an Action Expert in one policy, with task-state supervision used only in training.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Memory Expert architecture. Historical multi-view observations are encoded into history tokens, and future queries are appended to form the memory sequence. The sequence is processed with block-causal self-attention and conditioned on the instruction through cross-attention. During training, each token predicts its subtask and the state of every relevant object. The output of each Memory Expert layer conditions the corresponding Action Expert layer.
figures.headline: The Memory Expert turns multi-view history into tokens with appended future queries, and each token predicts subtask and object states during training.

abstract: Long-horizon embodied manipulation requires policies to act on information that is no longer visible. Modified objects may leave the field of view, while completed subtasks continue to constrain future actions. Existing approaches extend temporal context through recurrent state updates, test-time training, or storage and retrieval of past observations. As horizons grow, these mechanisms can still leave the policy to infer task state from long, redundant, and viewpoint-dependent visual experience. We argue that long-horizon agents benefit not merely from remembering more, but from remembering task-relevant state changes and progress. We propose Memory of Object States and Task Progress (MOST), a policy-internal memory framework that compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens. Historical and predictive future tokens are explicitly supervised with object states and subtask progress, structuring memory around what has changed in the world and what has already been accomplished. The resulting memory directly conditions action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage. We further introduce RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Across RoboCasa365, RoboCasa-Long, and real-world robot experiments, MOST consistently outperforms Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1), the previous state-of-the-art model. It raises average success from 65.9% to 72.1% on RoboCasa365, average maximum task progress from 20.83% to 42.22% on RoboCasa-Long, and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%. MOST also outperforms a matched visual-history memory variant, showing that effective long-horizon memory depends not only on how much experience is retained, but on whether it preserves decision-relevant progress and world-state changes.

sections.body: The introduction argues that long-horizon policies must preserve the task-relevant consequences of earlier actions, such as moved objects and completed subtasks, after they leave the current view. MOST pairs compressed multi-view memory tokens with subtask and object-state supervision, which is removed at inference. The section also introduces RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Reported results: average success rises from 65.9% to 72.1% on RoboCasa365, average maximum task progress from 20.83% to 42.22% on RoboCasa-Long, and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%. A matched visual-history variant is used to separate access to history from its representation.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Long-horizon manipulation needs object states and task progress kept after they leave view, so MOST stores them in policy memory.

sections.body: The related work groups prior methods into recurrence and attention, test-time training, compressed multi-frame memory, event retrieval, structured maps, and hierarchical planners. The section argues that these mainly address how history is retained or accessed. Task-state representations are the closest comparison: recurrent models, imagination-based memories, and object-centric memory. Planner-based task state, by contrast, is maintained outside the action policy. The section also reviews benchmarks including CALVIN, LIBERO, RoboCasa365, RoboMME, and RMBench. It states that RoboCasa-Long isolates persistent task state across several work areas.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior memory methods mainly vary how much history is kept, while MOST targets which task-state information persists.

sections.body: MOST has three parts: a Vision Language Model that encodes the current multi-view observation and instruction, a Memory Expert that converts sampled history into object-state and task-progress tokens, and an Action Expert that uses both through gated cross-attention. Each sampled timestep yields one history token, so memory growth does not depend on the number of views or image patches. Learned future queries are appended and supervised to predict the current subtask and the state of each relevant object. The auxiliary heads are removed at inference, while the memory and future queries remain active. The section notes that subtask and object-state vocabularies are closed-set and built from the training splits.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: MOST compresses multi-view observations into memory tokens supervised with subtask progress and object states, feeding actions directly.

sections.body: Experiments compare XR-1, a memoryless policy, with MOST-Raw, a visual-history variant without task-state supervision or future queries, and MOST, all under matched data and budgets. On RoboCasa365 Target-100%, average success is 65.9 for XR-1, 68.0 for MOST-Raw, and 72.1 for MOST. Tables 3 and 5 cover RoboCasa-Long and the real-world banana tasks, where average success is 36.66 for MOST-Raw and 43.33 for MOST, against 6.66 for XR-1. The section reports that MOST-Raw regresses on Target-100% Atomic tasks. Real-world evaluation uses 10 trials per task on a fixed base, so success rates are read together with progress metrics.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: MOST raises RoboCasa365 average success from 65.9% to 72.1% and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that MOST represents internal memory as the evolution of object states and task progress rather than as unstructured visual history. It attributes the results on RoboCasa365, RoboCasa-Long, and count-conditioned manipulation with a Galbot G1 to this representation for long and repetitive tasks. The stated limitations are closed-set state supervision, limited full-task success on the longest tasks, and a fixed-base real-world setting. Future work aims at more open-ended task-state abstractions and at tasks requiring navigation, manipulation, and longer-term adaptation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: MOST's gains suggest task-state memory helps long repetitive tasks, but success stays limited on the longest tasks.

sections.body: The appendix gives the Memory Expert configuration, with 384-dimensional tokens, 36 layers, a block size of 8, and 16 future queries. It also lists optimization settings, visual and temporal input timing, and the RoboCasa365 and RoboCasa-Long task setup. The real-world Galbot G1 setup uses 180 training demonstrations. It documents the task-state annotation format and the progress metric definitions, and notes that these differ from PRM-as-a-Judge 1.5 because no learned judge is used. Per-task RoboCasa365 Composite results are included.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists model, optimization, input timing, task setup, real-world setup, annotation format, and metric definitions.
